title: Christmas with family
hook: "Are you coming home for Christmas?" Yes, you can. Here's how to be there, keep your faith, and keep the peace.

screens.text: **Christmas is a week away,** and someone has probably asked already: "Are you coming home?" If you're new, this might be the moment you've been dreading. If you've been Muslim a while, you may have your answers ready. Either way: you can go, love your family, and stay true to your faith.

**Your bridge: Jesus.** Muslims love Jesus (**'Isa**) and Mary (**Maryam**). The Qur'an tells of the angels' news to Mary and the virgin birth [Q 3:45–47], and has a whole chapter named after her [Q 19:16–36].
bubbles: So when your family celebrates his birth, you share real common ground.
The difference: Muslims see him as a beloved prophet, not God's son [Q 4:171].

Not quite. Muslims love Jesus. Believing in him as a prophet is part of Islam.

screens.text: **What to do.** Keeping ties with your family is part of your faith [Q 31:14–15; Bukhari 2620]. So go home, help in the kitchen, enjoy the meal and the time together. Skip the religious rites: the worship, the prayers, the hymns.
bubbles: Scholars differ on saying "Merry Christmas" and on gifts. Ask your imam.

screens.prompt: Be there for it, or the part to skip?

items.why: Go. It's family time, and keeping ties is part of your faith. Just eat what's halal.
Yes. Help out, enjoy the time together.
That's worship, so it's the part to skip. If it's a big deal for your family, ask your imam before the day.
They're part of the worship, so they're the part to skip.

cards.back: Scholars differ: some allow it in words that don't go against your beliefs, others don't. Ask your imam.
Scholars differ on Christmas gifts too. Ask your imam. Whatever you decide, thank people warmly.

cards.front: The tree and decorations at your parents' house
cards.back: It's their home. You don't need to take anything down or comment on it. Whether to help decorate is a good question for your imam.

screens.character: Your mom (or dad) on the phone. Loving, excited to see you, a bit anxious about your new faith. Never cruel or threatening.
screens.setup: Your phone rings. "Hi, sweetheart! So, are you coming home for Christmas? Grandma's so excited. We're all going to the Christmas Eve service together, like always."
screens.goal: Say yes to coming home, show you're excited to see everyone, and kindly explain that you'll skip the service.
screens.success_looks_like: You say how much you want to be there, offer to help with dinner or stay with Grandma, explain briefly that you don't join church worship now, and keep the tone warm.
screens.coach_notes: The parent pushes: 'It's just one hour', 'Grandma will be heartbroken', 'You went every year', 'Is this the Muslims telling you what to do?'. They soften when the convert stresses love and offers something else (cooking, staying with Grandma, Christmas lunch). Never push the convert to join the worship. Debrief: one warm line, one firm-but-kind line, and a reminder that a calm 'no' to one thing and 'yes' to the rest is how ties stay strong. For teens, see the AI guide notes.

screens.text: **Your prayers.** Take your salah (prayer) with you: find a quiet room, step out for five minutes, and come back to the party.
bubbles: {teen}Under 18 and your parents expect you at church? Don't fight it out alone, and don't decide in the moment.{/teen}
{teen}Talk to {{mentor.name}} and your imam well before the day about what to do.{/teen}

screens.situation: At Christmas dinner, Grandma smiles at Ana: "Honey, would you say grace for us this year?" The family usually prays in Jesus's name.

options.text: Thank her, gently ask someone else to lead it, and sit quietly while they pray
options.feedback: Yes. Warm, honest, and no scene. Grandma feels honored, and Ana doesn't join a prayer she doesn't share.

options.text: Lead it in Jesus's name to keep the peace
options.feedback: Not quite. Muslims pray to Allah alone. Kindly passing the honor on keeps the peace and her faith.

options.text: Explain at the table why Muslims don't pray to Jesus
options.feedback: Not quite. A dinner-table debate hurts more than it helps. Save it for a calm moment, if they ask.

You can say "no" to one hour and "yes" to the whole visit. That's what keeping ties looks like.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Jesus and Mary in Islam (Day 27): the angels' news and virgin birth [Q 3:45–47]; Surah Maryam [Q 19:16–36]; Jesus a messenger and word of Allah, not His son [Q 4:171].
- Keeping ties with non-Muslim parents and family is part of the faith [Q 31:14–15; Bukhari 2620]; kindness and justice toward non-Muslims who aren't hostile [Q 60:8].
- Q5 drafted position: attend the family gathering and meal; don't take part in religious rites (services, prayers, hymns); don't resolve the greeting question; ask the imam. Range: SeekersGuidance (Hanafi) and IslamOnline (Badawi, Kutty) allow attending to keep ties without joining religious activities; Dar al-Ifta Egypt [6815] permits the greeting in words that don't contradict belief; IslamQA.info [947] prohibits the greeting, and [145986] says not to take part in any way, including parties and gift exchanges.

**Likely questions**
- *"How do I explain Jesus at Christmas?"* Common ground first: Muslims love Jesus, believe in the virgin birth and his miracles. The difference briefly: a prophet, not God's son. No debate.
- *"Can I say 'Merry Christmas'?"* Present both views (Dar al-Ifta Egypt permits; IslamQA.info prohibits) without choosing. Offer "Ask my imam." Warm alternatives: "Happy holidays to you too," "It's so good to see you."
- *"Gifts?"* Scholars differ on Christmas gifts. Don't resolve; "Ask my imam." Encourage gracious thanks whatever they decide.
- *"Church?"* Attending a relative's funeral is allowed (Day 77). Joining the worship itself is the part to skip under the drafted position. Suggest offering something else (cooking, staying with Grandma). A relative's funeral: attending and sitting respectfully is fine without joining the rites (Day 77). Adults asking about sitting through a wedding or Christmas Eve service: escalate. For a minor whose parents require attendance: don't coach defiance or deception; route to the mentor and imam before the day (Spec §6.2 rule 12).
- *"The food?"* Same as Thanksgiving: no pork or alcohol; meat per Q6, ask the imam.

**Escalate:** church attendance of any kind; greetings and gifts if they want a ruling; a minor required to attend church; family conflict that turns unsafe (safety rule).

**Don't**
- Don't rule on the greeting, gifts, or attendance.
- Don't mock Christmas, the Bible, the cross, or Christian worship.
- Don't tell anyone to skip the family visit.

**Role-play brief:** A loving parent on the phone, excited, a bit anxious; pushes on the Christmas Eve service and Grandma's feelings. Softens when the convert offers love and an alternative. Debrief on warm yes plus kind no.
